* **Task board:** TK-LJPWAR
* **Media:** M-DCNR86 (the setup screenshot, the Dream-1 run and the scripted demo are on the task board under this ID)
* **Category:** Societal relatability
Adds `tasks/robot-vacuum-brushroll/`: a task on the bimanual YAM station in Isaac Lab-Arena (`yam_arena`).

**Instruction:** Refit the brush roll in the robot vacuum's bay, with both of its ends seated, and then latch the red retainer flap down over the drive end.

The brush bay of a robot vacuum stands open with its retainer flap sprung up; the brush roll lies on the table in front of it. The robot picks the roll up by its body, carries it over the bay and lowers it so the 11 mm round stub enters the bearing slot and the 8 mm square stub the drive socket (45 degree lead-ins, a few mm of play), lets go, and pushes the retainer flap down until its latch catches. Scoring: roll lifted, both ends seated, retainer latched over the seated roll, grippers clear; 1.0 only after a second of stillness; 0 if the roll is lost or the retainer is latched on an empty bay.

- Run limit: 2,400 steps (2 minutes at 20 Hz)
- Scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2400 steps, hit the step limit); demo: 1.0 at step 530 (scripted demo, `--policy yam_scripted`)

Everything (assets, code, wording) was written for this task; nothing is taken from any earlier submission. Run commands, the scoring table and reset are in the task's README.



### Setup

info.body:
The robot opens the brush door of a robot vacuum for roller cleaning, the first step of the monthly brush clean in the maker's owner's guide ("Pinch the brush frame release tab, lift the tab"). An iRobot Roomba i7 (339 mm, 3.4 kg) lies upside down on the bench; at the end of its two rubber rollers a narrow hinged door covers their bearing ends, its far end held by a spring catch whose two green buttons stick out of either side of it in small finger recesses. One hand pinches the door's end, squeezing both buttons flush so the hooks under the recess floors come free, then turns with the door about its hinge until it stands open past upright, and lets go. Lifting the end without squeezing gets nowhere: in simulation, pads only touching the buttons slide off them, and a half squeeze (buttons 1.4 of 3.5 mm in) lifts the door 0.35 degrees before the tongues stop it and it drops shut; one button alone does not free it either. Full credit needs the door open at least 80 degrees, both hands 3 cm clear and everything still for 1 s, with the vacuum where it was; open 30 degrees or more scores 0.5, the catch released and the door lifted 5 degrees 0.25.

- task.json: instruction, setup, scoring, run limit and fidelity notes
- README.md: run and score commands, every collider, the scorer's conditions, the scripted demonstration, the simulation checks of the right and wrong ways, what is estimated
- open_robot_vacuum_brush_door.py: scene, scorer and scripted demonstration
- yam_parts.py, yam_joints.py, yam_linkage.py: kit modules, copied unchanged
- test_open_robot_vacuum_brush_door.py: CPU checks of the scorer on the start, the goal and partial and shortcut layouts

Scores: scripted demonstration 1.0; Dream-1 run 0.0 (the hands move about over and beside the vacuum; the door stays shut).

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

Revision addressing the review:
- **Buildable changer:** a manual changer of the locking-ring type, specified in the setup and in a new README section, "Building it for a real trial".
  - **Robot side:** a 64 mm steel flange on an ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 wrist mount, with two 6 mm locating dowels. A steel ring 88 mm across and 18 mm deep turns behind the face. - **Instruction:** it now states only the goal (fit and lock the blue suction tool, gripper tool left in the rack, let go, arms home), without prescribing which hand does what.

comments.body:
Revision addressing the review:
- **Clarity and reproducibility (not met):** the README has a new section, "Changer design (buildable)", and the setup
  summarizes it. It specifies a dimensioned manual locking-ring changer of the breech-lock type:
  - a section along the axis and a table of angles round it;
  - a parts table with sizes, fits, fixings and materials;
  - the lead-ins' range, a lever-movement table and force estimates.

  Every size is a constant in the task file, and the numbers in the text were printed from the code and compared. The
  scene now draws the claws, lugs, dowels, bushings, retaining disc and marks at those sizes.
- **Dowel locations:** two hardened 6 mm m6 dowels, 14 mm long, stand 6 mm out of the face, 22 mm from the axis. One is
  at 12 o'clock (round); the other is a diamond pin at 6 o'clock, its lands facing 3 and 9 o'clock. They are pressed
  8 mm into reamed 6 mm H7 holes. The tool plate takes them in two pressed, hardened bushings with 6 mm E8 bores (0.008
  to 0.034 mm clearance) and 1.5 mm lead-ins.
- **Mating cam and tool-lug dimensions and profiles:**
  - Lugs: the plate (60 mm across, 8 mm thick) has three lugs at 12, 4 and 8 o'clock. Each is 24 degrees wide
    (13.7 mm), runs from the rim (30 mm) to 36 mm from the axis, and is 3.0 mm thick, flush with the mating face.
  - Claws: the ring has three claws at 2, 6 and 10 o'clock, each 80 degrees of arc, reaching 11 mm in front of the
    face. Their lips are 32 to 38 mm from the axis. The 40-degree gaps pass the lugs with 8 degrees to spare.
  - Cam profile: each lip's back face starts from its leading end with a 1 x 45 degree chamfer. Then come a lead-in
    ramp over 12 degrees (from 9.0 to 3.6 mm in front of the face, 37 degrees), a clamp ramp over 5 degrees (to 2.8 mm,
    15 degrees) and a flat dwell over the remaining 63 degrees. The dwell overlaps the lugs' front faces (3.0 mm) by
    0.2 mm, giving about 16 N of clamp.
- **How the ring is mounted:** its 64 mm H7 bore turns on the flange's 64 mm g6 journal (0.010 to 0.059 mm clearance,
  greased), 4 to 22 mm behind the face.
- **How it is retained:**
  - In front, by the flange's 70 mm x 3 mm lip, through a 4-wave washer (64.5/69.5 mm, 0.45 mm strip, 1.0 mm high as
    fitted, about 12.5 N).
  - Behind, by a 76 mm x 4 mm steel retaining disc. The four M6 x 30 low-head screws (ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6, 50 mm circle)
    clamp it between the flange and the wrist.
  - The washer's friction (about 0.13 N m) keeps the ring where it is left, against the lever's weight (0.07 N m).
- **How it is stopped:** a hardened 4 mm pin in the retaining disc (35 mm from the axis, 12 o'clock) runs in a groove in
  the ring's back face, 4.2 mm wide and 4.5 mm deep. The groove's ends stop the ring at 1 degree past open and at 35
  degrees.
- **Locks and releases with the stated lever movement:** the lever is 110 mm long, with the pad's top 14 mm above its
  line.
  - Pressing the pad down 15.4 mm (8 degrees) brings the lips to the lugs.
  - 38.5 mm (20 degrees) draws the plate home.
  - 47.8 mm (25 degrees, the LOCK mark) pulls it tight onto the dwell. The stop is at 65.6 mm (35 degrees).
  - Lifting the pad back below 25 degrees slackens the clamp; below 8 degrees the tool comes off.
- **Simulation matched to the design** (code changed, so everything was re-run):
  - The scene draws the claws (their lead-in ramps as steps), lugs, dowels, bushings, the 70 mm face lip, the retaining
    disc and the marks.
  - Ring and lever now have their real mass: 661 g, centre of mass 10.8 mm toward the lever (it was 50 g, on the axis).
  - The seating window is now the lead-ins' range: face 6 mm, centre 6 mm (was 1 cm), tilt 9 degrees (was 12), turn 8
    degrees (was 20).
  - "Locked" needs the ring still at 25 degrees or more at the end. The lock lets go at 8 degrees, where the lugs line
    up with the gaps (it was 15).
  - The demo aims against its measured hold offset (3.5 mm and 4.5 mm).
- **Simulation approximation kept in the fidelity note** (481 characters): the claws, lugs and dowels are drawn but do
  not touch. Seating is a pose check over the lead-ins' range. The lock is a fixed joint, switched on at 25 degrees, that
  holds the tool square until 8 degrees; a real tool has play below 25. Ring friction is a moving-hold spring, without
  the clamp ramps' extra 0.2 N m.
- **Re-run:** scripted demo 1.0, Dream-1 0.0. One-hand check 0.25: the tool sat on the flange with the ring
  open, and fell when the hand let go.

Revision addressing the review:
- **Clarity and reproducibility (not met), the seating window:** the window now follows from the specified dowels and
  bushings, and the scorer checks exactly these numbers. Its constants are computed in the task file from the dowel
  and bushing sizes. The window counts only the bushings' 1.5 x 45 degree lead-in chamfers (1.5 mm wide, 1.5 mm deep).
  It leaves out the bores' 0.004 to 0.017 mm running clearance and the dowels' own ISO 8734 lead-in (about 1.2 mm on
  a 6 mm pin).
- **Lateral offset: 1.5 mm, was 6 mm.** It is now checked at each dowel. Each dowel's axis must be within 1.5 mm of its
  bushing's axis where it meets the plate's face, so the dowel's edge (3 mm from its axis) lands inside the chamfer's
  4.5 mm mouth radius. The round dowel is checked in every direction; the diamond pin across its lands. For a square,
  unturned plate this puts its middle within 1.5 mm of the axis. Because the check is made at each dowel, it also
  counts the turn, which moves each bushing 22 mm x sin(turn) sideways.
- **Tilt: 1.95 degrees, was 9.** The bushings are 44 mm apart. Both dowel tips are inside their 1.5 mm deep chamfers
  at once only while the tilt puts one bushing at most 1.5 mm nearer the face than the other: asin(1.5 / 44) = 1.95
  degrees. Tilted more, the nearer dowel enters its 0.008 to 0.034 mm clearance bore before the farther one is caught,
  and binds.
- **Face gap: 5.25 mm at the plate's middle, was 6 mm.** The dowels stand 6 mm out. At a 1.95 degree tilt the farther
  bushing is 22 x sin(1.95 degrees) = 0.75 mm farther out, so 6 - 0.75 = 5.25 mm keeps both tips in their chamfers.
- **Turn: 3.9 degrees, was 8:** asin(1.5 / 22) = 3.91 degrees.

Revision addressing the review:
- **Clarity and reproducibility (not met), the seating predicate:** the predicate is now geometric and depends on
  depth.
  - For each dowel, d is how far its tip has gone into the plate, e how far its axis is off the bushing's where it
    crosses the plate's face, and t the tilt.
  - A pose is accepted only while e + d tan t + 3 mm x (1/cos t - 1) <= 0.004 mm + max(0, 1.5 mm - d). This says the
    dowel's widest point at depth d stays inside the hole there.
  - In the 1.5 x 45 degree chamfer, the allowed offset is the chamfer's radius at that depth: 1.5 - d mm, plus 0.004 mm.
  - In the bore it is 0.004 mm, the smallest radial clearance of the 6 mm E8/m6 fit (0.008 to 0.034 mm on the
    diameter). The tilt is then held to about atan(0.004 mm / d).
  - Both dowels are checked in every direction as full 6 mm pins, at the tightest fit, without their own end
    chamfers, so every accepted pose fits every build within tolerance.
  - It also needs both tips past the plate's face, the plate's face nowhere past the flange's, every lug front within
    the lips' 10.0 mm reach, and, for the plate to go on, its lugs between the lips.
- **Couple the permitted offset and tilt to insertion depth:**
  - **Largest offset:** 1.404 mm at d = 0.1 mm, 1.104 mm at 0.4 mm, 0.504 mm at 1.0 mm, 0.104 mm at 1.4 mm, and
    0.004 mm from 1.5 mm on.
  - **Tilt in the bore:** at most about 0.05 degrees at d = 5 mm.
  - **The review's example is now rejected:** a plate 1 mm from the face has its dowels 5 mm in, so each must be
    within 0.004 mm. A 1 mm offset would intersect by 0.996 mm.
- **Every accepted pose physically achievable, checked against the geometry:**
  - The README section "What the dowels capture" gives the rule and tables printed from the task file:
    - the largest accepted offset at each gap;
    - tilted samples (gap, offset, tilt, each dowel's depth, need and room);
    - the review's example.
  - Every row is checked by an independent brute-force test: the dowel's surface, sampled every 1 degree and 0.1 mm,
    against the bushing's chamfer and bore.
  - At zero tilt the rule is exact: the clearance is 0 at the limit, and 0.01 mm further intersects by 10 µm.
  - Of 20,520 grid poses (gap 0 to 6.25 mm, offset 0 to 1.6 mm, tilt 0 to 3 degrees), 4,248 are accepted and none
    intersects (smallest clearance 0.08 µm).
  - Of 20,000 random poses (also turned, with the ring at 0 to 8 degrees), 2,762 are accepted and none intersects.
- **What the simulation does now:**
  - The drawn dowels cannot centre a plate, so an uncentred plate pushed past the chamfers is no longer accepted.
  - Two collision-only stops, 6 mm across and 5.6 mm out of the face, stand in for the dowels' tips: a pushed plate
    rests on them with the tips 0.4 mm into its chamfers.
  - When the ring passes 8 degrees, where its lips come over the lugs, it takes a tool seated there. A fixed joint
    holds the tool drawn home onto the face, centred and square, as a real ring's ramps do by 20 degrees. From 25
    degrees it counts as locked.
  - Before, a fixed box (offset 1.5 mm, gap 5.25 mm, tilt 1.95 degrees, turn 3.9 degrees) let the tool lock at 25
    degrees from wherever it was held.
- **Setup and fidelity note updated:**
  - The setup (3,786 characters) states the rule, the lug conditions, and the taking at 8 and locking at 25 degrees.
  - The fidelity note (485 characters) states the depth-coupled check, the stops and the fixed joint from 8 degrees.
  - The README also states that a real plate pushed past the chamfers is centred by them and then hangs on its dowels.
- **Full-score demo re-run under the corrected predicate:**
  - The holding wrist is now also pitched back 0.6 degrees (measured), so both dowel tips reach their chamfers.
  - While the plate sat on the tips with the ring open, d was 0.30 to 0.40 mm, e at most 0.78 mm against at least
    1.16 mm of room, and the tilt at most 0.17 degrees.
  - The ring took the tool at 8 degrees and locked it. The scripted demo scores 1.0 (394 steps).
  - Dream-1 scores 0.0: it reaches toward the suction tool and does not lift it.
  - The one-hand check scores 0.25: the tool sat seated on the tips with the ring open for 6 s, and fell when the hand
    let go.

Revision addressing the review:
- **Feasibility (not met), a full robot arm and a precision-machined steel changer with no affordable route:** the real
  trial now needs neither.
  - An unpowered printed wrist stand replaces the robot arm.
  - The changer is printed in PETG round bought precision parts; nothing is machined.
  - The priced parts come to $233.35, and the whole rig to about $300.
- **Low-cost inert wrist stand:** a printed pedestal with a 68 mm dummy wrist.
  - Its ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 face (four M6 heat-set inserts, a 31.6 mm recess, an orientation pin) holds the changer at
    the task's pose: axis 300 mm forward and 85 mm above the table.
  - It is bolted through an 18 mm plywood board held to the table by two C-clamps.
  - Drawings, an STL file and the parts are in the README. The simulated scene now shows this stand in place of the
    arm.
- **Affordable compatible changer by part number:** we checked catalogue manual changers (ATI MC-50, SCHUNK CMS 050,
  Destaco TC1, Milibar, OnRobot, OPT OC90 and others).
  - The only one shown to have both two alignment pins and a hand lever, the ATI MC-50, is sold on quote.
  - The priced ones cost $465 to $1,244, or show no dowels. The README tabulates them.
- **Fabrication-ready files and a low-cost build route:**
  - six dimensioned SVG drawings, made from the simulation's own constants;
  - 14 STL files covering all 16 printed pieces, in their print orientations;
  - a parts list with part numbers, links and prices, the masses, build steps and setup checks.
  - The hardened bushings are bonded in place on the flange's own dowels, so printing tolerance does not set the fit.
- **Two-dowel alignment preserved:** a round dowel (ISO 2338, 6 h8) and a diamond pin (DIN 6321 form C, 6 g6), 44 mm
  apart, in DIN 179 bushings (6 F7 bores) behind 1.5 x 45 degree lead-ins.
  - The seating rule now uses this fit's smallest radial clearance, 0.005 mm.
  - The brute-force geometry check was re-run: 4,318 of 20,520 grid poses and 2,926 of 20,000 random poses are
    accepted, and none intersects.
- **Manual locking action preserved:** the same three-claw ring and lever, cam (lead-in 9.0 to 3.6 mm over 12 degrees,
  clamp ramp to 2.8 mm over 5, dwell) and stops (1 degree past open, 35).
  - No wave washer of the earlier size is sold at its load, so six catalogue springs (Lee Spring LC 016A 01) preload
    the ring: 11.0 N at rest, 14.7 N clamping.
  - Checked on the STL solids: a plate passes the claws at 0 and 7.9 degrees and is blocked at 8.5. Locked, the lips
    overlap the lugs by exactly the 0.2 mm clamp travel.
- **Simulation consistent with the build, re-run:**
  - the stand replaces the arm, and the lip is 74 mm;
  - ring and lever now weigh 140.4 g (printed; they were 661 g of steel);
  - the tools' centres of mass come from their parts and ballast;
  - the status light is gone; the LOCK mark is the indicator;
  - the instruction names the tool flange on the wrist stand.
  - Demo 1.0 (358 steps). Dream-1 0.0: it moves the right hand to the rack and lifts neither tool. One-hand check
    0.25: the tool sat seated with the ring open for 5.5 s, then fell when let go.
- **Also added:** a "Why it matters" section tying the task to robot building on manual changers, and a "Real-trial
  safety and rig protection" section.

Revision addressing the review:

  • Feasibility (not met), a full robot arm and a precision-machined steel changer with no affordable route: the real
    trial now needs neither.
    • An unpowered printed wrist stand replaces the robot arm.
    • The changer is printed in PETG round bought precision parts; nothing is machined.
    • The priced parts come to $233.35, and the whole rig to about $300.
  • Low-cost inert wrist stand: a printed pedestal with a 68 mm dummy wrist.
    • Its ISO 9409-1-50-4-M6 face (four M6 heat-set inserts, a 31.6 mm recess, an orientation pin) holds the changer at
      the task's pose: axis 300 mm forward and 85 mm above the table.
    • It is bolted through an 18 mm plywood board held to the table by two C-clamps.
    • Drawings, an STL file and the parts are in the README. The simulated scene now shows this stand in place of the
      arm.

    Destaco TC1, Milibar, OnRobot, OPT OC90 and others).
